title: What Would You Say You Do Here?
subtitle: Make your role and scope explicit
summary: Pip’s new staff-engineer badge arrives with conflicting requests. Writing more code will not settle them. The role gains leverage through technical direction, judgment, and helping teams succeed. Pip compares actual work with the manager’s expectations, making communication, scope, and organizational context part of the technical job.

concepts.title: Scope
concepts.body: Pip’s badge says “staff,” but three teams read three different promises. Scope is the negotiated boundary of responsibility and influence, not a title’s hidden instruction manual. Pip and the manager write one sentence: which area to serve, which decisions to influence, and which gaps to fill. Another workshop may need a different staff role. The conversation establishes responsibility before the request queue establishes it by accident.

steps.text: Pip discovers that the title did not define the job.
A badge is not an agreement about responsibility.
Name the area, decisions, and gaps Pip will serve.

concepts.title: Judgment
concepts.body: A difficult bug tempts Pip away from an incident review. But colleagues need a decision under uncertainty: rollback or rewrite, with which constraints and consequences? Technical judgment joins the bigger picture, important execution, and helping others become capable. Pip explains why a rollback fits this situation, then helps the team act. Choosing where to contribute is part of the job; the hardest code is not always the most useful work.

steps.text: Pip chooses where judgment is most useful.
An incident creates uncertainty and constraints.
Help colleagues act rather than taking every hard task.

concepts.title: Communication
concepts.body: “Perhaps change the API,” Pip says. By lunch, three teams think that was an order. Influence travels farther than code. Pip replaces the ambiguous remark with a short note: context, suggestion, and the response needed. Questions, writing, and explanation are execution because they move understanding between people. A colleague can now proceed without another meeting—and can tell a possibility from an actual decision.

steps.text: Pip notices a suggestion being treated as a decision.
A colleague can proceed with shared understanding.

concepts.title: Role shape
concepts.body: Pip tries to imitate a celebrated staff engineer and spends the week in the wrong meetings. The workshop needs something different. Reporting chain, scope, preferred work, and primary focus do not always point together. Pip compares the agreed focus with requests arriving this quarter and names the mismatch. A staff role answers local organizational needs; negotiating its shape is more useful than copying someone else’s checklist.

steps.text: Pip checks whether the role still fits the workshop.
The written focus names an intended contribution.
Negotiate the mismatch instead of copying another engineer’s career.

misconceptions.claim: a staff-plus role is mainly about applying a universal formula.
misconceptions.correction: The chapter treats judgment as contextual: identify forces, listen to evidence, and adapt the response to the actual system and people.

misconceptions.claim: A visible activity or artifact proves the work is complete.
misconceptions.correction: Completion requires a useful outcome, shared understanding, and a way to notice whether the decision worked over time.

scenario.title: Name the role
scenario.context: Three workshop teams ask Pip for architecture, release help, and mentoring. The manager counts only Pip’s code. Which expectation should guide the work?

options.label: Clarify scope first
options.benefit: A shared focus lets teams know which decisions need Pip.
options.cost: Negotiation takes attention and exposes conflicting expectations.
options.consequence: Pip and the manager agree a primary focus and success signals; the teams know when to ask for help.

options.label: Accept every request
options.benefit: Every requester gets an immediate yes.
options.cost: The queue keeps competing with the manager’s success measure.
options.consequence: Pip appears responsive, but incompatible demands consume credibility and leave the hardest work without clear ownership.

scenario.debrief: Pip cannot resolve incompatible expectations through personal effort alone. A negotiated focus connects the workshop’s needs to accountable outcomes.

quiz.question: A newly promoted staff engineer receives incompatible requests. What should they clarify first?
options: Which request has the most difficult code
Their expected scope and current primary focus
Which colleague has the oldest ticket
quiz.explanation: The title does not determine the role; scope and organizational needs must be made explicit.

quiz.question: Which contribution fits the broader staff role?
options: Helping several teams make better decisions
Avoiding execution to focus only on strategy
quiz.explanation: The role joins bigger-picture work, execution, and enabling others.

quiz.question: Why might staff engineers at two companies have different jobs?
options: One must be using the title incorrectly
Organizations have different needs and structures
quiz.explanation: Role shape depends on the surrounding organization, not a universal checklist.

exercise.title: Make the next move legible
exercise.prompt: Describe a staff-level decision, the people and terrain involved, and the route by which you will learn whether it worked.

fields.label: Which expectation must be renegotiated?

fields.label: How will my manager and teams know it is working?
fields.placeholder: Name the evidence or conversation that will revisit it.
